# **Shared senescence-associated predicted expression and a bipolar-specific replication-maintenance layer: transcriptome-wide association distinguishes depressive overlap from illness identity**

## **Abstract**

**Background.** Major depressive disorder (MDD) and bipolar disorder (BIP) share depressive phenomenology and overlapping genetic liability, yet differ in polarity, longitudinal course, treatment priorities, and maintenance strategy. When the presenting episode is depression, the distinction may remain uncertain for years. Synaptic pruning, complement activation, and generic “accelerated aging” models have each been proposed as shared biological explanations, but none has yet produced a robust molecular separator between MDD and BIP.

**Methods.** We analysed stored S-PrediXcan results generated from the 2025 Psychiatric Genomics Consortium BIP genome-wide association study and the 2025 trans-ancestry MDD genome-wide association study. Associations were tested against eight prespecified gene sets covering cellular senescence, telomere maintenance, complement, synapse pruning, histocompatibility, and adult astrocyte, oligodendrocyte, and microglial markers. Gene-set results were partitioned into senescence-only, telomere-only, and overlapping components. We then applied gene-level quiet-majority tests, subunit ablation, leave-one-out influence analysis, split-half reliability, estimator sensitivity, tissue leave-one-out analysis, and chromosomal-arm checks. Stage-4 analyses interrogated stored Z scores only and did not rerun the underlying GWAS or eQTL analyses.

**Results.** Three set-level directions survived driver-drop: cellular-senescence-associated predicted expression was negative in both disorders, whereas telomere-maintenance predicted expression was negative in BIP only. The BIP telomere signal was located outside the overlap with the cellular-senescence set. It remained after removal of telomerase-biogenesis, shelterin/CST, polymerase/primase, and RNA polymerase II subunits; the residual was carried in substantial part by fork and lagging-strand genes. Quiet effects were modest: the BIP telomere-only genes had a mean Z of approximately −1.1 and a median near −1.0. MDD and BIP shared a stable nine-gene negative senescence-associated core comprising AGO1, ANAPC2, CDKN2D, CEBPB, ERF, IGFBP7, MAPK9, PHC2, and UBE2E1, embedded within a weaker tail. Quiet senescence-only genes agreed in sign in 58.7% of cases and had a Spearman correlation of 0.28. Pruning and complement signals collapsed under leave-k-out analysis.

**Conclusions.** The results support overlap without identity: a small shared senescence-associated predicted-expression core with loose node sharing, together with a BIP-specific replication-maintenance layer outside the senescence overlap. This architecture provides a candidate molecular rationale for depressive phenocopy and a frozen set of genes for future lithium-response and polarity studies. It is not a diagnostic test, does not measure RNA, telomere length, or enzyme activity in patients, and does not establish that mood disorders are pruning diseases.

**Keywords:** bipolar disorder; major depressive disorder; transcriptome-wide association study; S-PrediXcan; telomere maintenance; cellular senescence; lithium; diagnostic delay

## **1\. Introduction**

### **1.1 The clinical problem the genetics must speak to**

The clinical distinction between MDD and BIP is often made before the biology of the illness has declared itself \[1\]. Many people who later receive a bipolar diagnosis first seek treatment for depression, not mania or hypomania. In that setting, the symptoms that dominate the consultation are sadness, anhedonia, impaired sleep, altered appetite, reduced energy, anxiety, and suicidal thinking. These symptoms are not sufficient to distinguish bipolar depression from unipolar depression. The diagnosis may remain uncertain until a later episode, a more detailed longitudinal history, or a treatment-associated change in polarity makes the underlying course visible.

This delay is not simply a classificatory inconvenience. Systematic reviews indicate that the diagnosis and guideline-recommended treatment of bipolar disorder are often delayed for years, with depression as the first episode associated with longer periods of untreated or undiagnosed illness \[2\]. Prospective studies also show that a substantial minority of people initially diagnosed with MDD later meet criteria for bipolar disorder, particularly over extended follow-up \[3\]. Antidepressant-associated mood switching and diagnostic transition are clinically heterogeneous, but they remain part of the practical problem because treatment may occur before the illness trajectory is clear \[4,5\].

The harms of delayed recognition are specific. A patient whose illness is eventually understood as BIP may spend years receiving treatment designed for recurrent unipolar depression, while mood-stabilizing maintenance is delayed or omitted. Antidepressant monotherapy may be poorly matched to the longitudinal course of BIP and, in some patients, may be followed by treatment-emergent mania or hypomania. Lithium and selected atypical antipsychotics remain central to bipolar maintenance, but there is no laboratory assay that reliably distinguishes a patient experiencing MDD depression from a patient experiencing BIP depression while both are still depressed \[6\]. The unresolved clinical question is therefore not whether MDD and BIP share biology. They clearly do \[7\]. It is whether their overlap can be separated from the biology that gives the illnesses different courses.

The 2025 BIP genome-wide association study analysed 158,036 cases and approximately 2.8 million controls across multiple ancestries, identified 298 genome-wide significant loci, and reported enrichment involving GABAergic interneurons and medium spiny neurons \[8\]. The 2025 trans-ancestry MDD study analysed 688,808 cases and 4,364,225 controls, identified 697 associations at 635 loci, and reported enrichment involving postsynaptic density, receptor clustering, several neuronal populations, and antidepressant targets \[9\]. These studies provide sufficient genetic resolution to ask where shared liability ends and illness-specific liability begins.

### **1.2 Why pruning was a reasonable first hypothesis—and why it may not travel**

Synaptic pruning was a reasonable starting hypothesis because complement-dependent elimination of synapses is a well-established developmental mechanism. C1q and C3 participate in the tagging and removal of inappropriate synaptic connections, and microglia help sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity- and complement-dependent manner \[10,11\]. Complement component 4 has also been implicated in schizophrenia risk, giving the pathway a strong psychiatric genetics precedent \[12\].

The same biological vocabulary appears in the gene sets analysed here. The gene set labelled synapse pruning contains C1QA, C1QB, C1QC, C3, CX3CL1, CX3CR1, EPHA4, NGEF, SARM1, TREM2, and related genes. The Reactome complement cascade contains many of the same genes as well as C4A, CFH, CD46, SERPING1, and other complement regulators. If MDD and BIP shared a common, genetically driven over-pruning process, one would expect these sets to show a shared and driver-robust direction. If the process were present in only one disorder, it should remain after removal of the genes with the largest individual effects.

That is the hypothesis the original gene-set analysis was designed to test. The failure of pruning and complement to survive the robustness battery is therefore a result, not an uninformative negative sidebar. The relevant question is not whether complement can participate in synaptic elimination in the developing brain. It can. The question is whether the stored S-PrediXcan results support complement-mediated over-pruning as a module shared by MDD and BIP. They do not.

### **1.3 Why aging-adjacent sets were the second hypothesis**

Aging-related biology was a second plausible hypothesis because telomere length, cellular stress, inflammation, and cellular senescence have all been discussed in relation to mood disorders and broader aging biology \[13\]. Several observational studies have reported shorter leukocyte telomeres in bipolar disorder, although the evidence is heterogeneous and sensitive to sampling source, sex distribution, medication exposure, smoking, body mass index, illness burden, and assay choice. The results concern peripheral or cellular measures; they do not establish a brain-wide aging process.

Lithium adds a clinically relevant layer to this literature. Long-term lithium treatment has been associated with longer leukocyte telomeres in observational bipolar samples, and telomere length has differed between lithium-treated and never-treated patients in some studies \[14,15\]. Neither observation establishes that lithium acts through the replication-maintenance genes identified here, and neither converts a telomere association into a treatment biomarker. The appropriate interpretation is narrower: a BIP-specific replication-maintenance signal would be compatible with, but not evidence for, the possibility that cellular maintenance biology is relevant to lithium response.

Cellular senescence is not equivalent to telomere length. A senescence gene set can include cell-cycle regulators, chromatin proteins, Polycomb components, APC/C ubiquitination machinery, MAPK nodes, p53/RB components, and inflammatory or secretory genes. Telomerase activity can change without a measurable change in telomere length, and telomere length can vary without a canonical senescence program. The distinction is essential for the present analysis.

The analytic prediction was therefore explicit. If “accelerated aging” is a single shared factor, the intersection between telomere maintenance and cellular senescence should carry the principal signal. If BIP has an additional replication-maintenance component not shared by MDD, the telomere-only remainder should be negative in BIP and not in MDD. The partition between intersection, senescence-only genes, and telomere-only genes was designed to distinguish these possibilities rather than allowing a broad aging label to absorb them.

### **1.4 What TWAS can add to the clinic, tightly**

S-PrediXcan tests whether genetically predicted cis-regulated expression is associated with case status. The predicted expression is derived from genotype-based expression weights trained in reference transcriptome data; it is not directly measured RNA from a patient’s current depressive episode \[16,17\]. A negative Z score means that alleles associated with higher disorder risk tend, in the prediction model, to lower the genetically predicted expression of that gene. A large negative Stouffer statistic can therefore arise from many modest, directionally aligned gene-level associations.

This distinction matters throughout the manuscript. The current analysis does not measure RNA abundance in neurons, telomere length in blood or brain, telomerase activity, fork restart, cellular senescence, or treatment response. TWAS associations can also be affected by linkage disequilibrium, shared eQTLs, correlated prediction models, and use of a tissue that is not mechanistically relevant to the trait \[18,19\]. A significant TWAS result is consequently a candidate regulatory association, not proof that the implicated gene is causal.

The clinical value of this type of analysis, if replicated, would be more limited and more precise than a diagnostic classifier. It could provide a molecular account of why two depressive presentations overlap, identify a BIP-specific biological layer that MDD does not share, and define preregistered gene lists for the studies that are actually needed: lithium-response TWAS, treatment-emergent mania studies, BIP subtype analyses, and direct comparisons with schizophrenia.

### **1.5 Aim**

We tested whether genetically predicted expression in pruning, complement, senescence, telomere-maintenance, histocompatibility, and glial-marker gene sets was shared between MDD and BIP, specific to one disorder, or driven by a small number of influential genes. We then asked whether any surviving signal had the shape of a distributed quiet majority, a small stable core, a mismatch of nodes within a common process, or a set-level artefact.

## **2\. Methods**

### **2.1 Source GWAS**

The BIP input was derived from the multi-ancestry Psychiatric Genomics Consortium study by the Bipolar Disorder Working Group, which included 158,036 BIP cases and approximately 2.8 million controls and identified 298 genome-wide significant loci \[8\]. The MDD input was derived from the trans-ancestry Psychiatric Genomics Consortium study, which included 688,808 cases and 4,364,225 controls and identified 697 associations at 635 loci \[9\].

The downstream analyses reported here did not rerun either GWAS. They operated on stored S-PrediXcan results in the MDD and BIP input folders. The manuscript therefore treats the upstream summary-statistic and prediction-model provenance as part of the input dataset. The exact ancestry restriction and model-release metadata should be reported from the upstream input manifest. The supplied downstream code does not independently reconstruct those details.

### **2.2 TWAS and tissue-level results**

The stored analysis contained brain-tissue S-PrediXcan results for the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex BA24, hippocampus, caudate, nucleus accumbens, and frontal cortex BA9. For each disease, tissue-level gene Z scores were combined with a Stouffer procedure to obtain a meta-Z for each gene. The downstream pipeline also retained the individual tissue-level results for tissue-consistency and tissue leave-one-out analyses.

The analysis used genetically predicted expression rather than measured expression. The framework follows PrediXcan and summary-statistic TWAS methods, in which cis-genetic predictors are trained from reference transcriptomes and projected into GWAS summary data \[16,17,20\]. The GTEx v8 atlas provides the broader reference for tissue-specific genetic regulation and multi-tissue prediction, but the downstream scripts supplied for this manuscript did not independently verify the exact upstream model-release metadata \[21\]. That provenance should therefore be confirmed before submission.

### **2.3 Gene sets**

Eight prespecified gene sets were analysed. The Reactome cellular-senescence set contained 197 genes, the Reactome telomere-maintenance set contained 112 genes, the Reactome complement-cascade set contained 115 genes, and the GO biological-process synapse-pruning set contained 18 genes. The remaining sets were adult astrocyte markers containing 40 genes, adult oligodendrocyte markers containing 35 genes, adult microglia markers containing 25 genes, and an HGNC histocompatibility-complex group containing 44 genes.

The pruning set was labelled using an MSigDB 2025.1 description, whereas the Reactome sets were labelled with MSigDB 2026.1 descriptions in the supplied notebook. The glial-marker panels and histocompatibility set were custom or database-derived panels rather than de novo pathway definitions. The two aging-related Reactome sets share a large number of histone and telomere-associated genes. For that reason, the later analyses partitioned the sets into the intersection, senescence-only remainder, and telomere-only remainder. This partition was not an optional exploratory adjustment; it was necessary to prevent the shared portion of two overlapping gene sets from being misdescribed as an independent shared aging program.

### **2.4 Set-level statistics**

For each disease and gene set, the pipeline calculated a Stouffer Z, mean Z, median Z, mean absolute Z, trimmed mean, Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero, competitive permutation p value, and bootstrap confidence intervals when enabled (Figure 1). Pairwise MDD–BIP analyses included unpaired and paired tests, Cohen’s d, rank-biserial correlation, sign concordance, Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient, Kendall’s tau, Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, cosine similarity, and distance measures.

The run also performed gene-level leave-one-out influence analysis. A gene was flagged as influential when its removal changed the absolute Stouffer statistic by more than 20% or changed its sign. Global family-wise FDR was calculated across 152 p values generated within the run; 22 entries survived an FDR threshold of 0.05. These entries included enrichment, differential, profile-proximity, pairwise, and concordance tests. Because the p values were pooled across related analyses, the global FDR was treated as a claim-filtering device rather than as independent confirmation of a biological mechanism.

![][image2]

***Figure 1\. Analytical pipeline of the results-only transcriptome-wide association workflow.***

***(a) Inputs and predicted-expression layer.** Two independent case–control GWAS datasets are processed through S-PrediXcan, which projects genotype-based cis-expression weights into the summary statistics to yield stored gene × tissue Z scores across six brain regions. Tissue-level scores are combined by Stouffer's method into a single per-gene meta-Z for each disorder. Upstream summary-statistic, prediction-model, and ancestry provenance are logged from the input manifest; the downstream pipeline neither re-runs the GWAS nor the eQTL analyses.*

***(b) Prespecified gene sets and overlap-aware partition.** Eight gene sets are analysed, spanning aging biology (olive), immune and synaptic pathways (plum), and glial cell-type markers (ochre); bar length is schematic of relative set size. Because the senescence and telomere-maintenance sets share many genes, they are decomposed into an intersection, a senescence-only remainder, and a telomere-only remainder so that shared members are not misattributed to an independent aging program.*

***(c) Set- and gene-level statistics.** Each set is summarised by a Stouffer combined Z and a panel of complementary estimators with permutation and bootstrap inference. Leave-one-out influence analysis flags genes that dominate a set-level statistic. Results are then collapsed to one row per gene and bucketed by cross-disorder direction, and disorders are compared with paired/unpaired tests, effect sizes, and concordance metrics under a single global false-discovery correction.*

***(d) Staged robustness cascade.** Surviving associations pass sequentially through four escalating stages — driver-drop robustness, overlap-aware module testing, gene-centric architectural analysis, and an adversarial battery — each with prespecified decision gates that keep, narrow, or demote a claim. Every stage interrogates the stored Z matrix only; replication, colocalization, SMR, and cell-type-resolved TWAS require additional inputs and are not performed here.*

### **2.5 Gene-centric re-analysis**

Stage 3 collapsed the stored results into one row per gene, with one Z score for each disease and membership in the relevant gene sets. Genes were assigned to the telomere–senescence intersection, the telomere-only partition, the senescence-only partition, or the remaining gene pool. Additional buckets distinguished loud drivers, convergent significant genes, divergent significant genes, disease-private positive and negative genes, quiet concordant genes, and quiet discordant genes.

Telomere submodules were defined as shelterin/CST, telomerase biogenesis, helicase/remodeller, fork/lagging-strand biology, primase/replicative polymerases, RNA polymerase II, and other telomere-associated genes. Senescence submodules were defined as Polycomb, RB/p53, SASP/NFκB, MAPK, and shared shelterin genes. Quiet-majority analyses recalculated Stouffer statistics after removal of loud genes and after removal of the five genes with the largest absolute Z values. Signed hub pairing examined whether genes with similar signs in both diseases travelled with the same partners. Three frozen lists were generated for later work: shared\_aging\_neg, the BIP telomere-negative list, and aging\_divergent.

### **2.6 Robustness battery**

Stage 4 was prespecified to challenge four claims: that the BIP telomere-only signal was a distributed quiet majority, that MDD and BIP shared a senescence-associated core, that the shared layer involved different nodes rather than the same genes at different amplitudes, and that pruning or complement did not constitute an enriched module.

The battery included leave-k-out decay curves, subunit ablation, an estimator grid using Stouffer, mean, median, trimmed mean, and winsorized Stouffer statistics, random split-half analysis, leave-one-out testing of the nine-gene core, threshold sensitivity at absolute Z values of 1.0, 1.64, 1.96, and 2.58, tissue leave-one-out analysis, and chromosome-arm distribution checks. The decision rules were defined in advance: Claim 1 required at least six robustness tests to pass, Claim 2 required at least three, and Claim 4 required the pruning signal to fail the leave-k-out test. Stage 4 used stored Z scores only. It did not perform replication, colocalization, SMR, cell-type TWAS, lithium-response analysis, or treatment-emergent mania analysis.

## **3\. Results**

### **3.1 What the raw enrichment said—and what driver-drop deleted**

The raw analysis produced a strong negative BIP association for the full telomere-maintenance set. The full set contained 55 mapped genes in the enrichment table and had a Stouffer Z of −7.50, a permutation p value of 0.0024, and a Wilcoxon p value of 0.0104. The direction was consistent across the six brain-tissue streams: all six tissue-level telomere results for BIP were negative, with a mean tissue-level Z of approximately −2.97. Cellular senescence was negative in both disorders. The negative senescence direction remained after removal of influential genes, although it did not meet the stricter BIP quiet-majority rule described below.

Several apparent set-level findings were not robust. The BIP histocompatibility-complex association changed from a Stouffer Z of −5.49 to −0.38 after influential genes were removed. The MDD oligodendrocyte-marker result changed from \+4.01 to \+0.19, the MDD complement result from \+3.80 to \+1.89, and the BIP astrocyte-marker result from \+2.52 to \+1.07. The BIP complement result changed direction, from \+2.26 to −0.18, and the BIP oligodendrocyte result changed from \+2.02 to −0.16. The most influential genes included HLA-DMA and HLA-DMB for the histocompatibility set, GLYCTK for the oligodendrocyte set, C4A and CFH for complement, and SDC4, PRODH, and SLC14A1 for the astrocyte panel.

The principal full-set and driver-drop results are summarized in Table 1\.

| Gene set or claim | Disease | Full-set Z | Robust/driver-drop Z | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| REACTOME\_TELOMERE\_MAINTENANCE | BIP | −7.50 | −5.87 | Robust survivor |
| REACTOME\_CELLULAR\_SENESCENCE | BIP | −4.70 | −5.45 | Robust survivor |
| REACTOME\_CELLULAR\_SENESCENCE | MDD | −3.55 | −4.16 | Robust survivor |
| HGNC\_HISTOCOMPATIBILITY\_COMPLEX | BIP | −5.49 | −0.38 | Collapse |
| ADULT\_OLIGODENDROCYTE\_MARKERS | MDD | \+4.01 | \+0.19 | Collapse |
| REACTOME\_COMPLEMENT\_CASCADE | MDD | \+3.80 | \+1.89 | Collapse toward null |
| ADULT\_ASTROCYTE\_MARKERS | BIP | \+2.52 | \+1.07 | Collapse |
| REACTOME\_COMPLEMENT\_CASCADE | BIP | \+2.26 | −0.18 | Sign flip |
| ADULT\_OLIGODENDROCYTE\_MARKERS | BIP | \+2.02 | −0.16 | Sign flip |

The overlap-aware analysis separated the two aging-related Reactome sets. The intersection contained 56 genes and was near zero in both disorders, with Z values of −1.23 for BIP and \+0.51 for MDD. The telomere-only remainder was strongly negative in BIP, with Z \= −7.56, but weakly positive in MDD, with Z \= \+1.57. The senescence-only remainder was negative in both disorders, with Z \= −4.53 for BIP and −3.82 for MDD. This pattern is not consistent with a single shared aging factor. It separates a shared senescence-associated layer from a BIP-specific telomere-only layer.

The sets that most directly invite an immunological or pruning interpretation did not survive the first robustness filter. Their unadjusted enrichment values were influenced by a small number of genes, and the apparent direction was often not preserved after driver removal. The relevant conclusion is not that complement biology is irrelevant to the brain. It is that these data do not support a robust MDD–BIP pruning or complement module.

(Figure 1 near here: overlap-aware partition of the telomere and senescence sets, with full-set, intersection, and unique-remainder Stouffer statistics. Figure 2 near here: leave-one-out comparison of robust and fragile set-level claims.)

### **3.2 Finding 1: BIP carries a distributed replication-maintenance layer that MDD does not**

The lead result was located in telomere-maintenance genes that were not also members of the cellular-senescence set. The partition is the central observation. The negative BIP signal was not carried by the shelterin-and-histone block shared by the two Reactome lists. It was carried by the remainder: fork protection and C-strand fill-in, clamp loaders, primase and replicative polymerases, RNA polymerase II subunits, a helicase/remodeller fringe, and a smaller telomerase-biogenesis tail.

The quiet BIP-negative genes define the biology more accurately than the Reactome title. The fork and fill-in group included FEN1, LIG1, RFC5, PCNA, RPA1, DSCC1, and CHTF8. The primase and polymerase group included PRIM1, PRIM2, POLA2, and POLD1. The RNA polymerase II group included POLR2H, POLR2J, and POLR2D. The helicase/remodeller group included RUVBL1 and RTEL1. The quiet biogenesis tail included TERT, WRAP53, SHQ1, and GAR1, while CTC1 represented the CST fragment that remained among the quiet genes.

The individual gene patterns reinforced the distributed interpretation. PRIM1 was close to null in MDD and strongly negative in BIP, with MDD Z \= \+0.59 and BIP Z \= −5.79. FEN1 was negative in both disorders but stronger in BIP, with MDD Z \= −5.21 and BIP Z \= −8.24. POLR2H was also more negative in BIP, with MDD Z \= −1.69 and BIP Z \= −7.70. RTEL1 was inverted: positive in MDD and negative in BIP, with MDD Z \= \+2.47 and BIP Z \= −3.24. PPP6C was strongly positive in MDD but close to zero in BIP, with MDD Z \= \+9.41 and BIP Z \= \+0.78. It was therefore retained as a disease-private weight within the telomere list, not interpreted as part of the BIP program.

The ablation results showed that no single named telomere subunit was load-bearing. Removing shelterin/CST genes left a BIP Stouffer Z of −7.64. Removing telomerase-biogenesis genes left Z \= −7.21. Removing helicase/remodeller genes left Z \= −7.01. Removing the fork/lagging-strand group left Z \= −6.54, and removing the polymerase/primase group left Z \= −6.52. Most importantly, removing polymerase/primase and RNA polymerase II together still left a BIP Z of −5.21, with a quiet remainder of −4.15. The residual was therefore compatible with fork and lagging-strand biology even after the obvious polymerase and transcriptional subunits had been removed.

The overlap-aware partition and the corresponding quiet-majority results are summarized in Table 2\.

| Telomere–senescence intersection | 56 | \+0.51 | −1.23 | Not estimable | Not estimable | Does not carry the BIP signal |
| Telomere-only remainder | 56 | \+1.57 | −7.56 | −1.18 | −3.29 | BIP-specific negative layer |
| Senescence-only remainder | 141 | −3.82 | −4.53 | −3.42 | −4.21 | Shared negative layer with a weak tail |

The robustness battery converged on the same interpretation. After the five loudest genes were removed, the BIP telomere-only signal remained negative at Z \= −3.29, with 60% of the remaining genes negative. The associated binomial sign test was not significant, with p \= 0.222. This distinction matters. The robustness rule classified the signal as a pass because the direction, magnitude, and negative fraction were retained. The sign test does not support the sentence that most genes were individually negative beyond chance. The defensible sentence is that many modest predicted-expression associations point in the same direction.

The quiet-only aggregator grid gave a similar result. For BIP telomere-only genes, the Stouffer Z was −6.59, the mean was −1.13, the median was −0.97, the 10% trimmed mean was −0.93, and the winsorized Stouffer statistic was −6.34. The agreement in sign across estimators was stable, while the difference between the large Stouffer value and the mean or median showed that the combined statistic reflected directional coherence rather than a large typical gene-level effect. Random split-half sampling preserved the sign in 99.6% of 500 random halves, with a median absolute half-sample Stouffer value of 4.66.

The principal robustness checks for the BIP telomere-only result are summarized in Table 4\.

**Table 4\. Robustness checks for the BIP telomere-only layer**

| Robustness check | Result | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Removal of the five loudest genes | Z \= −3.29; negative fraction \= 0.60 | Direction and magnitude retained |
| Quiet-only Stouffer | Z \= −6.59 | Strong directional aggregation |
| Quiet-only mean | −1.13 | Negative average effect |
| Quiet-only median | −0.97 | Negative typical gene-level direction |
| 10% trimmed mean | −0.93 | Stable after trimming extremes |
| Winsorized Stouffer | Z \= −6.34 | Sign agrees with Stouffer |
| Random split-half reliability | 99.6% same-sign halves; median absolute half-Z \= 4.66 | High internal reliability |
| Tissue leave-one-out | 0 aging-set sign flips among 96 rows | No single stored tissue carries the direction |
| Largest chromosome-arm group | 17p: 3 of 24 mapped genes, 12% | No single-arm concentration |

The tissue and chromosomal checks reduced two alternative explanations. Across 96 tissue leave-one-out rows, four sign changes occurred across all analysed sets, but none occurred in the aging-related sets. Among the quiet BIP-negative telomere-only genes, the largest mapped chromosome-arm group was 17p, containing three genes: CTC1, RPA1, and WRAP53. This represented 3 of 24 mapped genes, or 12%, rather than a single-arm concentration. The result was therefore not one locus wearing many functional labels and not one limbic tissue carrying the entire direction.

MDD did not show the same layer. The MDD telomere-only remainder began weakly positive at Z \= \+1.57 and changed to −1.18 after the five loudest genes were removed. The asymmetry between MDD and BIP is the disease-identity component of the result. Shared depressive liability is not sufficient to explain a BIP-specific replication-maintenance shift.

Biologically, the genes that remain after ablation are involved in finishing replication, stabilising stalled forks, loading or recycling replication machinery, and filling in the telomere C-strand. They are not simply markers of senescence. This interpretation is compatible with observational reports of shorter leukocyte telomeres in some bipolar samples and with associations between lithium exposure and leukocyte telomere measures \[14,15\]. Compatibility is not evidence. The present analysis contains no lithium phenotype, no telomere-length GWAS, no cell-type-specific TWAS, and no patient-level replication assay.

(Figure 3 near here: leave-k-out curves for the telomere-only partition. Figure 4 near here: BIP subunit-ablation waterfall. Figure 5 near here: quiet BIP telomere-only genes, with Z scores and chromosome arms.)

### **3.3 Finding 2: MDD and BIP share a nine-gene senescence-associated core, not a senescence majority**

The shared result was smaller and had a different statistical shape. The stable core comprised AGO1, ANAPC2, CDKN2D, CEBPB, ERF, IGFBP7, MAPK9, PHC2, and UBE2E1. The nine-gene core had a Stouffer Z of approximately −10.17 in MDD and −12.89 in BIP. Removing any one member left both disorders strongly negative; across the nine leave-one-out analyses, the least negative remaining values were approximately −8.82 for MDD and −11.29 for BIP.

The core and its residual tail are summarized in Table 5\.

**Table 5\. Shared senescence-associated core and residual senescence-only signal**

| Component | n | MDD Stouffer Z | BIP Stouffer Z | Additional robustness result | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Nine-gene convergent core | 9 | −10.17 | −12.89 | Leave-one-gene-out values remained strongly negative | Stable shared core |
| Senescence-only remainder after core and named divergent genes | 83 | −1.73 | −2.37 | Negative fractions: 0.55 in MDD and 0.51 in BIP | Weak distributed tail |
| Full senescence-only partition | 141 | −3.82 | −4.53 | After top-five removal: −3.42 in MDD and −4.21 in BIP | Set-level negative direction |
| Convergent negative genes at |Z| ≥ 1.64 | 14 | — | — | Core remains detectable | Threshold-supported core |
| Convergent negative genes at |Z| ≥ 1.96 | 10 | — | — | Core contracts | Moderate threshold stability |
| Convergent negative genes at |Z| ≥ 2.58 | 6 | — | — | More stringent core | Narrower leading edge |

The composition of this core also constrained the biological interpretation. AGO1 is involved in RNA silencing. ANAPC2 and UBE2E1 sit within ubiquitin-dependent cell-cycle and APC/C-related processes. CDKN2D is an INK4-family inhibitor but is not CDKN2A or p16. CEBPB and ERF are transcriptional regulators, IGFBP7 is related to extracellular and IGF-associated signalling, and PHC2 is a Polycomb-associated chromatin regulator. MAPK9 was the MAPK node that belonged to the shared negative core. This is a selected slice of a senescence annotation, biased toward chromatin, RNA regulation, ubiquitin, and transcriptional restraint rather than a canonical execution program.

The result was not p16 lock-in. CDKN2A moved in the opposite direction in BIP. Nor was it an RB/p53 block: the RB/p53 submodule was near zero in BIP and only weakly negative in MDD. The SASP/NFκB submodule was null to positive. MAPK1 was jointly positive, MAPK3 was a BIP-specific positive outlier, and MAPKAPK3 was an MDD-specific positive outlier. The words “MAPK cascade” and “senescence pathway” are too broad to describe the observed list.

The remainder of the senescence-only set formed a weak tail. When the nine-gene core and named divergent genes were removed, 83 genes remained; their Stouffer statistics were −1.73 in MDD and −2.37 in BIP, with negative fractions of 0.55 and 0.51, respectively. The direction was retained, but the majority criterion was not. In the leave-five-out analysis, senescence-only values changed from −3.82 to −3.43 in MDD and from −4.53 to −4.21 in BIP. BIP had 53% negative genes after the drop, below the prespecified 60% threshold. Thus, the full senescence-only direction survived in the sense of a distributed negative Stouffer shift, but it did not become a BIP quiet majority equivalent to the telomere-only finding.

Threshold sensitivity supported a core rather than a broad leading edge. The number of convergent negative genes was 14 at an absolute Z threshold of 1.64, 10 at 1.96, and six at 2.58. A negative core existed across conventional thresholds, while the size of the shared set-level leading edge contracted as the threshold became more stringent. That is the reason the shared finding should be called a core with a weak tail rather than a shared senescence majority.

(Figure 6 near here: per-gene Z scores for the nine-gene core with leave-one-gene-out values. Figure 7 near here: threshold sensitivity of the convergent-negative bucket.)

### **3.4 Finding 3: The shared layer is not the same nodes at different amplitude**

The quiet senescence-only profile contained 92 genes. MDD and BIP agreed in sign for 58.7% of these genes, and the quiet-profile Spearman correlation was 0.28. These values are sufficient to support a shared process-level layer, but not a shared gene-level vector.

The mismatch was not produced solely by the loudest outliers. NFKB1 was negative in MDD and positive in BIP. RTEL1 was positive in MDD and negative in BIP. EED and PHC2 diverged within the Polycomb-related component, and POLD2 showed opposite-direction behaviour within the polymerase block. The rank-inversion analysis also identified large swaps involving ABCA8, A2M, RPA2, PRODH, CLTCL1, SERPING1, POLD2, and FOLH1.

The distinction between set-level profile similarity and node-level agreement is important. Some gene-set profiles had positive Pearson correlations, including the telomere-maintenance profile, with r \= 0.407, and the complement profile, with r \= 0.568. The MHC profile was more tightly correlated, with r \= 0.730 and Spearman rho \= 0.815, although its BIP enrichment was driver-dependent. Profile correlation can therefore be moderate or high while the quiet genes responsible for the shared direction remain only loosely aligned. The disease model should preserve both observations: the processes overlap, but the nodes are not interchangeable.

The most restrained formulation is that MDD and BIP touch a common predicted-expression layer with partially different gene configurations. This is not the same as saying that BIP is MDD with a larger coefficient on one aging vector. It is also not a molecular account of mania, mixed states, or antidepressant-associated switching, none of which was analysed.

### **3.5 Finding 4: Pruning and complement are not modules**

The negative pruning result closed the original GMT hypothesis as a mechanism-level claim. In the pruning-like composite, the MDD Stouffer value changed from \+3.97 to \+0.92 after the five loudest genes were removed. The BIP value changed from \+2.09 to −0.63. The direction was not preserved, and the sign tests were not supportive.

The genes that initially invited the pruning interpretation were leverage points. These included NGEF, EPHA4, C1QA, ADGRB3, VANGL2, C3, and C1QB. Complement was similarly influenced by C4A and CFH. These genes can be reported as individual TWAS associations when scientifically appropriate. They cannot carry a sentence about genetically predicted over-pruning or complement activation as a disease-wide program.

The main robustness verdicts are summarized in Table 6\.

**Table 6\. Stage-4 robustness scoreboard and manuscript-level verdicts**

| Claim | Robustness result | Verdict |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| BIP telomere-only quiet majority | 8 of 8 tests passed | Keep |
| BIP signal is not only telomerase-related | Telomerase-biogenesis ablation remained negative | Keep |
| BIP signal is not only shelterin/CST-related | Shelterin/CST ablation remained negative | Keep |
| BIP signal is carried by polymerase/fork biology | Polymerase/primase plus RNA polymerase II ablation remained negative | Keep |
| Shared senescence-associated core | 4 of 5 prespecified tests passed | Keep |
| Shared layer has different nodes rather than identical amplitudes | Quiet Spearman rho \= 0.28; same-sign rate \= 58.7% | Keep |
| Pruning/complement as an enriched module | Leave-k-out survival failed | Demote; do not reopen |

The gene-level comparison nonetheless showed configuration differences. C1QA was near zero in MDD and negative in BIP, ADGRB3 was positive in MDD and near zero in BIP, EPHA4 was negative in MDD and positive in BIP, and NGEF was positive in both but more strongly positive in BIP. These patterns are suitable for a future treatment-emergent mania or plasticity analysis. They are not evidence that the pruning gene set survived as a module.

### **3.6 What was not tested**

The analysis contained no polarity-specific phenotype, no distinction between BIP-I and BIP-II in the S-PrediXcan folders, no treatment-emergent mania phenotype, no lithium-response GWAS, no schizophrenia S-PrediXcan folder, no educational-attainment Z column, and no sex- or age-at-onset-stratified analysis. Cycling and mixed states were also outside the data. The frozen lists generated by Stage 3 are therefore hypotheses for future work, not results from the present study.

The principal frozen lists were the shared aging-negative list, the BIP telomere-negative list, and the aging-divergent list. A broader BIP-extra telomere-maintenance candidate list contained 18 quiet genes, whereas the stricter frozen BIP telomere-negative list contained 11 genes at the suggested threshold. These lists should be treated as preregistered inputs for replication, colocalization, SMR, lithium-response analyses, and treatment-emergent mania studies.

## **4\. Discussion**

### **4.1 A model of overlap without identity**

The clinical problem is depressive phenocopy. Two patients may both meet criteria for a depressive episode while their illnesses differ in polarity, recurrence pattern, pharmacological response, and long-term maintenance needs. The current predicted-expression map provides a molecular shape for that clinical observation (Figure 2).

First, MDD and BIP both touched a senescence-associated predicted-expression layer. The most stable object within that layer was a nine-gene negative core involving RNA silencing, APC/C and ubiquitin-related processes, chromatin regulation, transcriptional restraint, IGF-associated signalling, and one MAPK node. Second, the two disorders did not touch that layer with the same genes. Quiet senescence-only genes agreed in sign only 58.7% of the time and correlated at rho \= 0.28. Third, BIP carried an additional negative layer in telomere-maintenance genes outside the senescence overlap. This layer was distributed across fork, fill-in, clamp-loader, primase, polymerase, RNA polymerase II, and helicase/remodeller biology, and MDD did not share its direction.

![][image3]

***Figure 2\. Proposed molecular architecture of the four non-interchangeable findings.***

***(a) A bipolar-specific replication-maintenance layer.** Schematic of a telomere/replication fork highlighting the machinery implicated outside the senescence overlap: fork protection and C-strand fill-in, clamp loading, primase and replicative polymerases, RNA-polymerase-II subunits, a helicase/remodeller fringe, and a faint telomerase-biogenesis tail. The model is one of directional coherence — many modest predicted-expression reductions pointing the same way (downward arrows) — rather than large effects at a few genes; the shelterin block and a simple "telomerase-off" mechanism are excluded (struck labels).*

***(b) A shared senescence-associated core.** The jointly implicated genes cluster around Polycomb repression, APC/C ubiquitin ligation, RNA silencing, an INK4-family CDK inhibitor distinct from p16, C/EBP–ETS transcriptional restraint, an IGF-binding secretome neighbour, and a single JNK-family node. This compact core sits against a weak, diffuse remainder (faint dots). Canonical senescence execution — p16 lock-in, the p53/RB block, and the SASP/NF-κB cassette — is not part of the shared object (struck labels).*

***(c) Overlap without identity.** Both disorders connect to a shared senescence-associated process layer, but through partly different molecular nodes (shared, MDD-leaning, and BIP-leaning dots), i.e. a common layer rather than the same genes scaled up. A second replication-maintenance layer is engaged by bipolar disorder only; the corresponding major-depression connection is absent (grey dashed stub, ✕).*

***(d) A closed synaptic-pruning hypothesis.** Complement tagging (C1q/C3) and microglial engulfment of synapses are shown as the original candidate mechanism. The enclosing module ring is broken to indicate that the pruning/complement set does not survive leave-k-out robustness testing (✕ gate); only isolated single-gene associations remain, which cannot support a pathway-level claim.*

This is a better account of overlap without identity than the statement that BIP is MDD with a larger aging coefficient. It is also a better account than a single “accelerated aging” factor because the intersection between senescence and telomere maintenance did not carry the BIP signal. The result is not that one illness is old and the other is young. It is that different predicted-expression processes are represented in the two disorders, with one process partly shared and another more prominent in BIP.

The interpretation is complementary to the large GWAS papers rather than competitive with them. O’Connell and colleagues identified BIP associations involving several neuronal cell types, including interneurons and medium spiny neurons. The MDD study identified neuronal, postsynaptic, receptor-clustering, and antidepressant-target signals \[8,9\]. Those results describe where disorder liability is enriched at the level of cells, circuits, and genes. The present analysis asks which maintenance-related predicted-expression programs those liability alleles appear to influence within a prespecified panel. Neither level replaces the other.

The map still does not classify a patient. A high or low gene-set Stouffer statistic is not a clinical probability of BIP, and the present Z values cannot be used as a case-level classifier. The correct translational claim is narrower: the genetic architecture contains a shared layer and an additional BIP-associated layer, and that is the shape a future classifier would need to test.

### **4.2 What the BIP layer is biologically—and what it is not**

The residual telomere-only signal is most compatible with replication maintenance rather than with a simple “TERT-off” model. Fork and lagging-strand genes such as FEN1, LIG1, RFC5, PCNA, and RPA1 participate in the processing of replication intermediates and Okazaki fragments. CST-associated genes contribute to telomere replication and replication restart after fork stalling. RTEL1 and related helicase or remodeller components help manage difficult telomeric structures. These functions concern the completion and protection of DNA replication, including the telomere C-strand, rather than a single senescence marker \[22-30\].

The ablation results are important because they narrowed the claim. Removing telomerase-biogenesis genes did not remove the BIP signal. Removing shelterin/CST did not remove it. Removing polymerase/primase and RNA polymerase II together did not remove it either. Fork-associated genes continued to carry the direction. The manuscript should therefore avoid the phrases “telomerase suppression,” “shelterin failure,” or “polymerase shutdown.” They are too specific for the data.

The results are compatible with reports of shorter leukocyte telomeres in some bipolar samples and with observational associations between lithium exposure and longer leukocyte telomeres \[14,15\]. They do not show that BIP patients have shorter telomeres, because telomere length was not measured. They do not show that the implicated genes alter telomere length, because no mediation or colocalization analysis was performed. They do not show that lithium normalizes any of the predicted-expression associations. The direction of inference must remain one-way: the TWAS result motivates a maintenance hypothesis; the observational telomere and lithium literature provides compatibility; neither validates the other.

### **4.3 Why the shared core is the right size for a depressive-liability layer**

The nine-gene core is small enough to be interpreted and stable enough to survive individual-gene removal. Its composition also discourages an overly literal reading of the senescence label. The core does not represent all canonical senescence machinery. It does not behave like p16 lock-in, an RB/p53 block, or an IL6/NFκB secretory cassette. It is better described as a selected regulatory slice of a senescence-associated gene set.

That distinction is important because cellular senescence is a heterogeneous cell state, not a single transcriptional switch. Senescence-associated phenotypes can differ by cell type, initiating stress, duration, chromatin context, and secretory program \[31-33\]. A negative TWAS signal in a senescence gene set therefore cannot be translated directly into “senescent cells in the cortex” or “accelerated brain aging.” The current result is a genetically predicted-expression association with a selected regulatory layer.

The weak tail matters, but it should not be promoted to a second module. After the nine-gene core was removed, the residual senescence-only genes remained slightly negative in both disorders. That persistence explains why the full set-level Stouffer remained negative. The failure of the strict majority test in BIP explains why the tail should not be described as a quiet majority. The shared object is the core and its weak remainder, not a uniform set-wide suppression of senescence genes.

### **4.4 Translation 1: candidate biology for the lithium problem**

Lithium remains a central maintenance treatment for BIP because it reduces recurrence risk and has evidence relevant to suicide prevention, despite its monitoring burden and renal and thyroid costs \[6,34\]. The field still lacks a reliable pretreatment biomarker that identifies who will respond well. The current analysis does not solve that problem. It does, however, provide a defined candidate list that is biologically adjacent to an existing observational literature.

The quiet BIP telomere-only list is a reasonable candidate set for a lithium-response TWAS because it is BIP-specific within the present comparison, survives multiple robustness tests, and is enriched for replication-maintenance functions rather than for a single telomerase gene. The appropriate next analyses are concrete. Existing lithium-response GWAS or pharmacogenomic datasets could be tested against the frozen BIP maintenance list. Colocalization or SMR could be applied to FEN1, PRIM1, POLR2H, RTEL1, WRAP53, and related genes. In cellular models from lithium responders and non-responders, investigators could measure replication-fork restart, replication-stress markers, C-strand fill-in, telomerase activity, and telomere length separately.

The present manuscript should not claim that lithium works by restoring PRIM1, FEN1, or any other gene in the list. That is a testable hypothesis, not a result. The important contribution is the frozen candidate set and the decision to test replication maintenance directly rather than treating telomere length as a sufficient proxy.

### **4.5 Translation 2: a molecular rationale for phenocopy depression, not a test**

Current clinical assessment already uses family history, age at onset, recurrence, mixed features, sleep changes, prior treatment response, and collateral history to estimate bipolarity in a depressed patient. None is a definitive biological separator. The present analysis offers a proof of principle for a future molecular approach: predicted-expression space can contain both a shared depressive layer and a BIP-extra layer.

That does not mean that the current genes can be used to determine whether an individual patient has BIP. The analysis was performed on summary Z scores from case-control GWAS, not on patient-level symptom scores. There were no polarity labels, no longitudinal transitions, no treatment histories, and no individual-level predictor validation. A classifier built from these values would overstate the evidence and would be vulnerable to the same linkage disequilibrium, tissue, and prediction-model limitations that affect TWAS itself.

The correct clinical interpretation is therefore architectural. A future biomarker will probably need to capture both the shared depressive liability and the additional BIP-related biology. A score based only on shared senescence-associated genes would not be sufficient. A score based only on the BIP telomere-only list would also be incomplete. Both layers would require validation in independent cohorts with longitudinal polarity and treatment outcomes.

### **4.6 Translation 3: switching and polarity stay off-stage**

Treatment-emergent mania remains an important future phenotype, but it was not analysed here. The present study contains no antidepressant exposure variable, no switch phenotype, and no longitudinal record. The discordant complement and plasticity genes therefore define a candidate substrate list, not a switching mechanism.

This distinction is particularly important because the largest differences included loud genes such as EPHA4, NGEF, C1QA, ADGRB3, SERPING1, and CFH. Stage 4 showed that loud leverage points can generate apparent pathway-level effects that disappear under leave-k-out analysis. These genes may be useful in a preregistered treatment-emergent mania analysis, but they should not be used as the mechanistic explanation of switching in the present manuscript.

### **4.7 Why pruning must be retired as the mood-disorder headline**

The complement and pruning literature remains biologically valid. Complement-mediated synaptic elimination is established in developmental neurobiology, and C4 is a credible schizophrenia risk mechanism \[10-12\]. The current result does not challenge those findings.

It does show that those findings should not be transferred automatically to MDD and BIP. In this analysis, pruning-like enrichment did not survive the removal of the largest genes. Complement enrichment was similarly unstable, and the overlap between complement and pruning was too small to support an independent module. The genes can remain as individual TWAS associations or as candidates for future plasticity studies. The pathway claim should be retired.

Keeping pruning in the abstract as the shared mood-disorder mechanism would therefore repeat a narrative the robustness battery rejected. The correct negative conclusion is stronger than “we did not replicate pruning.” The data show that the apparent set effect had the structure of a driver-sensitive association, precisely the type of result that leave-k-out analysis is intended to expose.

### **4.8 Limits**

The primary limitation is that this was a predicted-expression analysis. S-PrediXcan does not measure RNA in living patients, does not establish disease-state expression, and does not identify telomere length or cellular senescence. The direction of a Z score refers to the genetically predicted component of expression under a reference model. The results should therefore be described as associations involving genetically regulated expression.

Second, TWAS associations are not automatically causal. Linkage disequilibrium can create associations at non-causal genes, correlated eQTL weights can produce multiple hits at one locus, and a reference tissue can be poorly matched to the disease-relevant cell type \[18,19\]. Colocalization, SMR, fine-mapping, and functional perturbation are required before any gene is promoted from candidate to causal mechanism. The present Stage-4 analysis did not perform those tests.

Third, the gene sets were prespecified but not independent. The telomere and senescence sets share genes, histone families, and annotation structure. The partitioning strategy reduced this problem but did not eliminate gene-set annotation bias. Stouffer aggregation also treats gene-level observations more simply than the underlying correlation structure warrants. Linkage disequilibrium, shared eQTLs, and cross-tissue prediction correlations can affect both the null distribution and the interpretation of a large combined statistic.

Fourth, the analysis was not a cell-type TWAS. Brain-tissue results were consistent across the six stored tissue streams for several aging-related directions, but the data do not identify the cell type in which the relevant regulatory effects operate. The BIP GWAS implicates interneurons and medium spiny neurons, but this analysis did not test those cell types directly.

Fifth, the disease phenotypes were broad case-control GWAS outcomes. There were no polarity strata, BIP-I versus BIP-II comparison, age-at-onset groups, sex-stratified estimates, mixed-state measures, rapid cycling, educational attainment, disability, lithium response, antidepressant switching, or schizophrenia comparison. Those absences are not minor details. They define the boundary of the clinical claims.

Finally, Stage 4 strengthened internal robustness but did not provide external replication. The same stored Z matrix was interrogated repeatedly with different partitions and sensitivity rules. The results therefore answer which sentences are load-bearing within this analysis. They do not establish that the same partitions will survive in an independent GWAS, a different prediction panel, a different ancestry composition, or a direct patient-level molecular experiment.

## **5\. Conclusion**

MDD and BIP are not represented by the same aging signature at different amplitudes, and they are not supported here as complement-pruning diseases.

They share a small, leave-one-gene-out-stable senescence-associated core, with a weak negative tail whose genes only loosely match between disorders. BIP also shows a distributed negative layer in telomere-maintenance genes outside the senescence overlap. That layer remains after the removal of telomerase-biogenesis, shelterin/CST, polymerase/primase, and RNA polymerase II subunits. Fork and lagging-strand biology can still carry the direction when the obvious polymerase genes are removed.

This split is the principal translational object. It gives a molecular shape to depressive phenocopy, identifies a candidate maintenance list for the unresolved lithium-response problem, and closes the case for pruning as the shared mood-disorder mechanism in this dataset. It does not diagnose an individual patient, prove that BIP is associated with short telomeres, establish a lithium mechanism, or explain mania. Those questions remain open, but they are now attached to frozen gene lists and specific next experiments rather than to an undifferentiated aging or plasticity narrative.

## **Integrated conclusions**

**Table A36. Final manuscript-level conclusions supported by the supplied analyses**

| Conclusion | Evidence | Status |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| REACTOME\_CELLULAR\_SENESCENCE is robustly negative in both diseases | Stage-2 driver-drop survivors; Stage-3 quiet-majority survival; Stage-4 aggregator and core-LOO stability | Keep |
| REACTOME\_TELOMERE\_MAINTENANCE is robustly negative in bip | Stage-2 robust survivor; Stage-3 bip telo-only quiet majority; Stage-4 8/8 tests pass | Keep |
| The bip telomere-only signal is not merely telomerase-off | Telomerase-biogenesis, shelterin, pol, and pol2 ablations retain negative signal | Keep |
| The shared senescence signal is distributed rather than dependent on the 12 convergent genes | Stage-4 senescence-only-minus-core test remains negative for both diseases | Keep |
| mdd and bip share a layer but not tightly aligned gene-level configurations | Quiet same-sign rate=58.70%; quiet Spearman ρ=+0.28; rank inversions and divergent/private genes | Keep |
| Complement/pruning should not be described as an enriched pathway | Driver-drop collapse/sign flips; leave-k-out failure; module tests and Stage-4 C4 pass | Keep |
| C1QA and C3 are candidate cross-set mechanisms | Stage-2 cross-set hub frequency | Follow-up only |
| Mania, lithium response, SCZ comparison, EA effects, cycling, sex, and age-of-onset mechanisms | Required GWAS/TWAS, eQTL, treatment-response, or stratified inputs are absent | Not testable here |

**Table A37. Explicitly blocked or untestable hypotheses**

| Hypothesis | Why blocked | Required future input |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Mania versus depression | No polarity phenotype in the TWAS folders | BD-I versus BD-II versus mania-only GWAS |
| AD-induced switching | No treatment or TEM phenotype | TEM/AD-response GWAS and switch-substrate list |
| Lithium specificity | No lithium-response GWAS | Lithium-response TWAS restricted to maintenance candidates |
| BD-I approximately SCZ greater than MDD | No SCZ S-PrediXcan folder | PGC3-SCZ TWAS rerun |
| EA sign flip versus disability | No EA Z column | EA TWAS projection of the same genes |
| Cycling or mixed states | Cross-sectional case-control Z only | Rapid-cycling or mixed-feature GWAS |
| Sex or age at onset | Unstratified meta-Z values | Sex-split or age-of-onset-split S-PrediXcan |
